A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Learn2Mix work. All 21 pages of v2 and 33 pages of v3, including equations, figures, tables, proofs, and appendices, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original classification, regression, and image-reconstruction experiments, with numerical outcomes in Tables 1–2 and Figures 2–3.

after.justification: Section 4 reports original experimental results, and Appendix B adds architecture and hyperparameter studies, worst-class accuracy comparisons, and mixing-parameter trajectories.

M1.justification: The loss-based mixing update, class-specific batch construction, cyclic sample reuse, and Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged. The added MobileNet evaluations use the same Learn2Mix procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same nine datasets across classification, regression, and reconstruction, with identical dataset descriptions and imbalance constructions. Appendix B of v2 becomes Appendix C of v3. The added studies vary settings and metrics within retained data and tasks.

E2.justification: Table 1 and Figure 2 expand every classification comparison from classical, focal/FCL, and SMOTE training to include importance sampling (IS) and curriculum learning (CURR). These are evaluated comparators, with implementations described in Appendices D.5–D.6. Regression and reconstruction retain classical training as their comparator.

E3.justification: Classification comparisons switch from epoch budgets to elapsed-time budgets, such as MNIST changing from 60 epochs to 50 seconds. Table 3 changes learning rates for MNIST, Fashion MNIST, and CIFAR-10; the main CIFAR-100 evaluation changes to MobileNet-V3 Small. Appendix B introduces architecture, optimizer, batch-size and learning-rate settings, plus worst-class accuracy evaluation.

E4.justification: New Appendix B investigates sensitivity to architecture, optimizer, batch size, learning rate, and mixing rate. Figures 4–7 examine convergence and worst-class accuracy, while Figure 8 tracks whether mixing parameters stabilize and prioritize difficult classes. These substantive analyses were absent from v2.

E5.justification: Both versions already display numerical uncertainty and shaded bands. The new checklist, item 7, explicitly describes the intervals as confidence intervals. This adds a reporting characterization, but supplies no confidence level, calculation method, seed information, or run count and does not establish additional runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the classification results under revised settings and adds IS/CURR entries. For example, final CIFAR-100 Learn2Mix accuracy changes from 17.02% with the larger LeNet-5 at 120 epochs to 54.50% with MobileNet-V3 Small at 200 seconds; these are different-condition results. Appendix B adds further findings, while Table 2's regression and reconstruction values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Learn2Mix's definitions, convergence propositions, corollary, and Appendix A proofs retain the same mathematical content. Equations 65–67 add mathematical definitions of IS sampling probabilities and loss, and CURR pacing and loss, to formalize the newly evaluated baselines.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: adaptive class proportions accelerate convergence across classification, regression, and reconstruction, supported by conditional theoretical results and experiments. The expanded evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix B adds interpretations connecting worst-class gains and mixing trajectories to emphasis on difficult classes, and discusses relative insensitivity to mixing-rate choices. The practical mixing-rate recommendation narrows from [0.01, 0.5] to [0.01, 0.1]. The existing reduced-overfitting explanation is retained.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands reproducibility information through MobileNet-V3 Small layer descriptions, IS subsampling details, CURR scoring and pacing parameters, and additional experiment settings. It newly identifies the RTX 3090 GPU and discloses exclusion of CURR's preliminary training from reported timings. The underlying repository link remains the same.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for importance sampling, curriculum training, MobileNet-V3, and RMSProp, including Katharopoulos and Fleuret, Johansson and Lindberg, Hacohen and Weinshall, Howard et al., and Graves. Related work now explicitly includes importance sampling, while the central novelty positioning remains unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 tightens and rephrases retained prose, adds an explanation after Equation 3, and updates author and funding text. It inserts the empirical appendix and checklist and renumbers retained appendices, while preserving the main five-section sequence and most existing exposition.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two-column to single-column NeurIPS formatting. Figure 2 is redrawn with classification-error versus elapsed-time axes and additional comparator curves; Table 1 expands, tables gain red highlights, and Figures 4–8 are added. Table 2 and Figure 3 retain their results but are restyled and repositioned.

improvement.justification: Elapsed-time comparisons directly strengthen the practical training-speed claim that v2 supported mainly through epoch-based comparisons. Added IS/CURR baselines and Appendix B's sensitivity, worst-class, and mixing-trajectory analyses substantially improve empirical scrutiny. These gains outweigh local reporting problems, including Figure 5's conflicting batch sizes of 150 versus 250 and incomplete confidence-interval specifications.
